Q: Seasonal Arthritis Guide: Managing Symptoms Through the UK Y
A: Managing arthritis symptoms year-round involves adapting to seasonal changes. In spring and autumn, layer clothing to combat fluctuating temperatures. Stay hydrated in summer, aiming for 2 litres daily, and protect sun-sensitive skin. To ease winter stiffness, use heated blankets and warm showers. Consistent medication and tracking symptoms are important year-round to pre-empt flare-ups.

## Expert Q&A: Should You Start DMARDs at Diagnosis?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-should-you-start-dmards-at-diagnosis
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Expert Q&A: Should You Start DMARDs at Diagnosis?
A: Starting disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drugs (DMARDs) early in inflammatory arthritis can slow disease progression, reduce joint damage, and improve long-term physical function. This is because there is a critical 'window of opportunity' in the early stages where DMARDs are most effective. Prompt treatment within this window can prevent irreversible damage and lead to a better quality of life.

## Gardening with Arthritis – UK Tips & Adapted Tools
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-gardening-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Gardening with Arthritis – UK Tips & Adapted Tools
A: Gardening with arthritis is achievable by using adapted tools and techniques. Ergonomic hand tools, long-handled tools, and ratchet secateurs reduce strain. Raised garden beds eliminate bending and kneeling. Pacing yourself by taking breaks, spreading tasks, and alternating positions also helps. Carrying items close to your body and using foam grips on tools are joint-friendly techniques to minimise discomfort.

## Omega-3 and Fish Oil for Arthritis: A Complete Evidence-Base
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-omega-3-fish-oil
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Omega-3 and Fish Oil for Arthritis: A Complete Evidence-Base
A: Omega-3 fatty acids, particularly EPA, help manage arthritis by reducing inflammation. They combat inflammation by displacing pro-inflammatory fats, producing anti-inflammatory molecules, and inhibiting inflammatory gene expression. For rheumatoid arthritis, take 2,000–3,000 mg of combined EPA+DHA daily, which can reduce pain, stiffness, and potentially lower the need for NSAIDs. Benefits appear within 2 to 3 months.

## Arthritis and Sleep Problems: How to Get Better Rest with Jo
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-sleep-problems
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Arthritis and Sleep Problems: How to Get Better Rest with Jo
A: Arthritis pain, inflammatory cytokines, and medication side effects can disrupt sleep. To improve sleep, ensure your mattress is medium-firm with good support, replace it every 7–10 years, and use pillows for spinal alignment. Sleep in a cool room (16–18°C), maintain a consistent sleep schedule, and create a calm wind-down routine. Avoid caffeine after 2 pm and time pain relief before bed.

## Arthritis and Weight Loss UK: How Losing Weight Helps Your J
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-and-weight-loss-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Arthritis and Weight Loss UK: How Losing Weight Helps Your J
A: For arthritis sufferers, even a small amount of weight loss can significantly reduce joint pain and improve function. Losing 1kg of body weight can reduce knee joint loading by 4kg during walking. A 5-10% reduction in body weight over 3-6 months is an achievable goal, with sustainable weight loss of 0.5-1kg per week being recommended.

## Managing Arthritis Fatigue – A UK Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/arthritis-fatigue-management-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Managing Arthritis Fatigue – A UK Guide
A: Arthritis fatigue is an overwhelming exhaustion not fully relieved by rest, affecting concentration, mood, and motivation. It differs from normal tiredness and can be as debilitating as pain. Inflammation, pain, poor sleep, anaemia, specific medications, reduced fitness, and the emotional burden of chronic illness all contribute to this profound fatigue. Energy management techniques like prioritising, planning, pacing, positioning, and self-permission can help.

## Natural Pain Relief for Arthritis: Evidence-Based Home Remed

## Best Exercises for Back Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiothera
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/back-arthritis-exercises-uk

Q: Best Exercises for Back Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiothera
A: Exercise is a core treatment for back arthritis, offering significant pain reduction comparable to medication. Recommended exercises include deep-core strengthening (pelvic tilts, bird-dog, glute bridges), spinal mobility (cat-cow, knee-to-chest), and low-impact aerobic activities like walking, cycling, or swimming. These help nourish discs, strengthen stabilising muscles, and improve posture without accelerating spinal degeneration.

## Hip Arthritis Symptoms UK: Signs, Diagnosis and Treatment Op

Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Hip Arthritis Symptoms UK: Signs, Diagnosis and Treatment Op
A: Hip arthritis symptoms typically develop gradually, often including groin pain that may radiate down the front of the thigh, stiffness, and reduced range of motion. You may also experience pain during or after activity, night pain, limping, and referred knee pain. If these symptoms persist for several weeks or worsen, see your GP.

## Hydrotherapy for Arthritis UK: Benefits, Access and What to 
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/hydrotherapy-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Hydrotherapy for Arthritis UK: Benefits, Access and What to 
A: Hydrotherapy is exercising in warm water, typically 33–36°C, helping arthritis by reducing body weight, allowing easier movement. The warmth relaxes muscles and lessens pain, while water resistance builds strength. NHS sessions, usually 30–45 minutes, are led by a physiotherapist, with courses often lasting 6–12 weeks. Access is usually via GP or rheumatologist referral.

## Best Exercises for Knee Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiothera
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/knee-arthritis-exercises-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Best Exercises for Knee Arthritis: A Complete UK Physiothera
A: Regular exercise is crucial for managing knee arthritis, reducing pain by 25–50% on average, strengthening supporting muscles, and improving flexibility. A balanced programme includes strengthening exercises (2-3 times/week), such as straight leg raises and wall sits, alongside flexibility exercises daily and 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly, like walking or swimming. Controlled joint loading helps nourish cartilage without worsening arthritis.

## Occupational Therapy for Arthritis in the UK
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/occupational-therapy-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Occupational Therapy for Arthritis in the UK
A: Occupational therapists (OTs) help people with arthritis maintain independence in daily activities. They teach techniques for joint protection, make custom splints, and recommend home adaptations such as grab rails and kitchen aids. OTs also assist with energy management, helping to balance activity and rest. You can access OT services through your GP, rheumatology department, or local council in the UK.

## Osteoarthritis Symptoms & When to See Your GP
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/osteoarthritis-symptoms-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Osteoarthritis Symptoms & When to See Your GP
A: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis, affecting millions. It occurs when cartilage cushioning bone ends wears down. Symptoms develop slowly and include joint pain, stiffness, swelling, and reduced movement. Common affected joints are the knees, hips, hands, lower back, and neck. See a GP if symptoms persist for weeks, worsen, or affect daily activities.

## Best Diet for Rheumatoid Arthritis UK: Evidence-Based Nutrit
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/rheumatoid-arthritis-diet-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Best Diet for Rheumatoid Arthritis UK: Evidence-Based Nutrit
A: The Mediterranean diet is recommended for managing Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA) and involves daily staples like extra-virgin olive oil, 5–7 portions of vegetables, 2–3 portions of fruit, whole grains, legumes, and nuts and seeds. Weekly priorities include oily fish 2–3 times and poultry and eggs. Foods to limit or avoid include processed items, added sugars, red meat, refined carbohydrates, and potentially alcohol and excess salt.

## Shoulder Arthritis Exercises: A Complete UK Physiotherapy Gu
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/shoulder-arthritis-exercises-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Shoulder Arthritis Exercises: A Complete UK Physiotherapy Gu
A: Shoulder arthritis exercises can significantly reduce pain and improve movement, benefiting conditions like osteoarthritis, rheumatoid arthritis, or post-traumatic arthritis. Key exercises include pendulum swings, wall crawls, and behind-the-back reaches to improve range of motion. Gentle strengthening can be achieved with resistance band external rotations, shoulder blade squeezes, and wall press-ups. Always warm up, move gently, and stop if you experience sharp or worsening pain.

## Spinal Arthritis and Back Pain UK: Symptoms, Treatment and S
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/spinal-arthritis-back-pain-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Spinal Arthritis and Back Pain UK: Symptoms, Treatment and S
A: Spinal arthritis, also known as spondylosis, affects the facet joints, discs, and vertebrae of the spine, causing chronic back and neck pain. Symptoms include stiffness, reduced flexibility, and pain that improves with gentle movement. Management involves exercises such as pelvic tilts and chin tucks, maintaining good posture, and sometimes physiotherapy or pain medication. Seek urgent medical attention for loss of bladder/bowel control or sudden weakness.

## Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: UK Guide to Cold-We
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/staying-active-arthritis-winter-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Staying Active with Arthritis in Winter: UK Guide to Cold-We
A: In winter, all adults in the UK should take a daily 10-microgram (400 IU) vitamin D supplement, as recommended by Public Health England. This is because between October and March, the UK does not receive enough sunlight for the body to produce sufficient vitamin D, which is vital for bone health, immune function, and may help reduce arthritis inflammation.

## TENS Machines for Arthritis UK: Do They Work and How to Use 
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/tens-machines-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: TENS Machines for Arthritis UK: Do They Work and How to Use 
A: TENS machines are drug-free devices that deliver mild electrical impulses through pads on the skin, a popular choice for arthritis pain relief. They work by stimulating nerves to "close the gate" on pain signals (high frequency, 80-120 Hz) and by triggering endorphin release (low frequency, 2-5 Hz). Evidence suggests short-term pain relief, but they are best used as part of a wider pain management plan.

## Walking Aids and Gadgets for Arthritis UK: A Complete Guide

Q: Walking Aids and Gadgets for Arthritis UK: A Complete Guide
A: Walking sticks reduce load on an affected hip or knee by up to 25%, while Nordic walking poles, used in pairs, can reduce lower limb joint loading by up to 30%. Rollators, available through NHS physiotherapy referral, offer more support with a seat. Wheelchairs and scooters assist with longer distances. Many aids can be provided free via an NHS occupational therapy referral.

## Expert Q&A: Why Did My Arthritis Come Back?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/expert-qa-why-did-my-arthritis-come-back
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Expert Q&A: Why Did My Arthritis Come Back?
A: Arthritis can reappear after stopping treatment because many people experience improved symptoms, prompting them to reduce or stop medication. However, stopping effective arthritis medication is clearly linked to symptoms returning or worsening, especially for inflammatory types. Maintaining a stable treatment plan, even during quiet periods, often leads to better long-term outcomes and helps prevent joint damage.

## Flare Management: What to Do When Pain Spikes
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/flare-management-pain-spikes
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Flare Management: What to Do When Pain Spikes
A: Flare management involves practical steps to reduce pain spikes. Gentle movement, aiming for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, and an anti-inflammatory diet, such as a Mediterranean pattern, can help. Weight management, applying heat for stiffness or cold for swelling for 20 minutes, and prioritising sleep hygiene are also beneficial. Clinical advice should be sought for sudden hot, red, swollen joints or prolonged morning stiffness.

## Gene Therapy and Arthritis: Where Are We in 2026?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/gene-therapy-and-arthritis-where-are-we-in-2026
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Gene Therapy and Arthritis: Where Are We in 2026?
A: Gene therapy for common forms of arthritis, such as osteoarthritis and rheumatoid arthritis, is not currently a standard treatment option in the UK. Research is in early stages, with most approaches being preclinical or in small human trials. Current robust evidence continues to support established treatments like appropriate drug therapies, regular physical activity, and supportive lifestyle measures for managing arthritis symptoms.

## Understanding Frailty in Older Adults
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/understanding-frailty-older-adults
Last updated: 2026-06-21
Q: Understanding Frailty in Older Adults
A: Frailty is a medical syndrome characterised by reduced strength, endurance, and physiological reserve, making individuals vulnerable to illness or injury. It is different from normal ageing, as many older people remain robust. Clinically, frailty is identified by unintentional weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slow walking speed, and low physical activity. Early identification is crucial for effective intervention and improved outcomes.

## Ginger Root: A Natural Anti-Inflammatory Food
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/ginger-root-natural-anti-inflammatory
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Ginger Root: A Natural Anti-Inflammatory Food
A: Ginger contains gingerols and shogaols that dampen the same COX-2 and cytokine pathways NSAIDs act on. Meta-analyses show a modest but real reduction in pain and stiffness in knee osteoarthritis, typically over 4–12 weeks at 500–1,000 mg/day of standardised extract, or 1–2 g/day of fresh root. Effect size is smaller than turmeric but tolerability is excellent.

## Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips

Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Managing Methotrexate Side Effects: Practical Tips
A: Common methotrexate side effects like nausea, fatigue, and mouth ulcers are often manageable. Taking prescribed folic acid significantly reduces these. If you experience new or concerning symptoms, such as sudden joint pain, fever, yellowing skin, or persistent vomiting, contact your doctor. Never stop methotrexate suddenly without consulting your care team due to the risk of disease flares.

## Why Morning Knee Stiffness Lasts 30+ Minutes

A: Morning knee stiffness lasting over 30 minutes is often due to arthritis, affecting either inflammatory or degenerative forms differently. Movement, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, and heat/cold applications can help. Aim for 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly and prioritise consistent sleep. Seek medical advice if stiffness lasts over an hour for more than two weeks, or if you have sudden hot, swollen joints.

## NHS Access to Biologics: How the Approval Pathway Works
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/nhs-access-to-biologics-how-the-approval-pathway-works
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: NHS Access to Biologics: How the Approval Pathway Works
A: Biologics for inflammatory arthritis are considered under UK guidance, usually when conventional DMARDs have not worked adequately, with DAS28 helping assess disease activity and guide treat-to-target decisions. Evidence from trials and reviews supports earlier targeted therapy for slowing joint damage and improving quality of life, while regular monitoring helps manage infection risk, side effects and treatment response.

## NSAID Stomach Protection: When You Need a PPI
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/nsaid-stomach-protection-when-you-need-a-ppi
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: NSAID Stomach Protection: When You Need a PPI
A: Combining a proton pump inhibitor (PPI) like omeprazole with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) significantly reduces the risk of gastrointestinal side effects including stomach ulcers and bleeding. This co-prescription is recommended for individuals at increased risk, such as those with a history of stomach problems, older adults, and those taking blood-thinning medications. PPIs offer vital protection when taking NSAIDs long-term or at higher doses.

## NSAIDs and Arthritis: Benefits, Risks and Safer Use
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/nsaids-and-arthritis-benefits-risks-and-safer-use
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: NSAIDs and Arthritis: Benefits, Risks and Safer Use
A: NSAIDs effectively reduce arthritis pain and stiffness, with benefits often appearing within hours to days, though responses vary. Use the lowest effective dose for the shortest duration, as side effects on the digestive system and kidneys become more likely with higher doses and longer-term use. Topical NSAIDs may offer localised relief with fewer systemic side effects.

## Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis — Understanding the Differences
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/oa-vs-ra-comparison
Last updated: 2026-06-16
Q: Osteoarthritis vs Rheumatoid Arthritis — Understanding the Differences
A: Osteoarthritis (OA) and rheumatoid arthritis (RA) both cause joint pain but differ fundamentally. OA involves cartilage breakdown, usually from wear and tear, and commonly affects knees, hips, and hands. RA is an autoimmune disease where the immune system attacks joint linings, causing inflammation and damage — typically symmetrical, often starting in smaller joints on both sides of the body.

## Paracetamol for Arthritis Pain: What the Evidence Says
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/paracetamol-for-arthritis-pain-what-the-evidence-says
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Paracetamol for Arthritis Pain: What the Evidence Says
A: Current evidence suggests paracetamol alone provides limited benefit for many with arthritis pain, especially for long-term conditions like osteoarthritis. While some studies show a small pain reduction compared to a placebo, this is often insufficient for daily life. It is generally recommended for mild pain or occasional flare-ups, usually in conjunction with other treatments, rather than as a primary, standalone solution.

## Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fi
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/shoulder-arthroscopy-and-arthritis-what-it-can-and-cant-fix
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Shoulder Arthroscopy and Arthritis: What It Can and Can't Fi
A: Shoulder arthroscopy will not cure arthritis or reverse joint damage. Evidence shows short-term benefits for some impingement, but it is not significantly better than non-surgical approaches long-term. For moderate to severe arthritis, arthroscopy offers little lasting benefit. It is typically reserved for specific situations when conservative methods like physical therapy, medication, and injections have failed.

## Shoulder Pain When Reaching: RA vs OA Differences
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/shoulder-pain-reaching-ra-vs-oa
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Shoulder Pain When Reaching: RA vs OA Differences
A: Inflammatory arthritis typically worsens with rest and improves with gentle movement. Degenerative arthritis, such as osteoarthritis, generally worsens with prolonged use. Recommended approaches include 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold applications, and good sleep hygiene. Seek medical advice for sudden hot, red, swollen joints, unexplained weight loss, morning stiffness over an hour for two weeks, or new numbness or weakness.

## Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/steroid-injections-vs-oral-steroids-when-each-makes-sense
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Steroid Injections vs Oral Steroids: When Each Makes Sense
A: Steroid injections typically alleviate pain and inflammation in specific joints for several weeks to months, often taking a few days to a week to become effective. Oral steroids are generally used for widespread inflammation. Neither is a long-term solution, and both carry risks with overuse. They should be part of a broader management strategy including exercise, therapy, and weight management.

## Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/stopping-arthritis-medication-safely-a-step-by-step-guide
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Stopping Arthritis Medication Safely: A Step-By-Step Guide
A: Stopping arthritis medication should always be a joint decision with your rheumatologist, even if you feel well. Abruptly stopping or significantly reducing effective treatments for inflammatory arthritis can increase flare-up risk and potential joint damage. It is a gradual process, often taking months, with consistent symptom monitoring throughout. If symptoms return, contact your care team promptly.

## Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/strength-training-on-biologics-is-it-safe
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Strength Training on Biologics: Is It Safe?
A: Strength training is generally safe and recommended for people with arthritis, even those on biologics. Research shows it can improve muscle strength, reduce pain, and boost physical function. It's crucial to start slowly, focus on proper form, and listen to your body, stopping if you experience new or lasting joint pain. Always discuss your exercise plan with your clinician.

Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Supporting a Partner With Arthritis: A Practical Handbook
A: The post says partners can support someone with arthritis through small daily acts, open communication and practical help with joint-straining tasks. It stresses clinician-led, personalised care combining medication, regular comfortable movement, symptom tracking and lifestyle support. It advises pacing, not stopping prescribed treatment, avoiding quick fixes, and seeking prompt review for swelling, fever, severe pain or rapid loss of function.

## Full-Body Low-Impact Workout: Swimming for Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/swimming-full-body-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Full-Body Low-Impact Workout: Swimming for Arthritis
A: Arthritis pain can arise from joints, surrounding tissues and the nervous system, with inflammatory and degenerative types behaving differently. The guide says structured movement, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, heat or cold, and good sleep can help. Start small, track pain and function weekly, and seek GP or physiotherapist advice for swollen red joints, weight loss, prolonged stiffness, numbness or weakness.

Q: Talking to Children About Your Arthritis
A: The article advises honest, age-appropriate conversations with children about arthritis, giving simple reassurance to younger children and more detail to older ones. It says clear communication can reduce worry and support family coping. Avoid hiding the condition, overwhelming medical detail, blame or false promises; invite questions and seek clinical advice for worsening symptoms, new concerns or overwhelm.

## Tapering Biologics: What the Latest Trials Show
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/tapering-biologics-what-the-latest-trials-show
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Tapering Biologics: What the Latest Trials Show
A: For people with well-controlled inflammatory arthritis, reviews of randomised trials show that a gradual reduction in biologic medication dosage can be considered. This involves spacing out injections or reducing the dose while maintaining disease control. Any tapering strategy should be highly individualised, carefully monitored, and undertaken in close consultation with a specialist to balance disease control with reduced side effects and cost.

## Thumb Base Pain: Early Signs of Hand Arthritis
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/thumb-base-pain-early-hand-arthritis
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Thumb Base Pain: Early Signs of Hand Arthritis
A: Thumb base pain can indicate early hand arthritis, which may be inflammatory or degenerative. Inflammatory arthritis often improves with movement, while degenerative arthritis can worsen with prolonged use. Effective management includes 150 minutes of weekly moderate exercise, anti-inflammatory eating, weight management, and heat or cold applications. Seek medical advice for sudden joint swelling, unexplained weight loss, prolonged morning stiffness, or new numbness.

## Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/topical-nsaids-often-overlooked-often-effective
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Topical NSAIDs: Often Overlooked, Often Effective
A: Topical anti-inflammatory gels and creams can be effective for joint pain, particularly in hands and knees. They deliver pain relief locally with fewer systemic side effects than oral medications. Use them regularly, 2-3 times daily, applying enough product as advised in the leaflet. Avoid use on broken skin, and consult a doctor if pain worsens or new symptoms appear.

## Total Knee Replacement: A UK Patient's Guide for 2026
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/total-knee-replacement-a-uk-patients-guide-for-2026
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Total Knee Replacement: A UK Patient's Guide for 2026
A: For many, non-surgical methods effectively manage knee pain. Tailored exercise, weight management, and pain relief consistently delay or avoid surgery. A 'stepped care' approach recommends starting with less invasive treatments, progressing only if needed. Patient satisfaction after knee replacement is highest when non-surgical options are explored and individuals are prepared.

## Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/walking-30-minutes-a-day-while-on-dmards-a-practical-plan
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Walking 30 Minutes a Day While on DMARDs: A Practical Plan
A: Walking daily with arthritis is generally safe and recommended, especially when gentle and progressive. Regular, moderate intensity exercise, including walking, improves joint function, reduces pain, and boosts overall quality of life. Tailored activity, alongside medication, helps keep muscles strong and supports heart health. Listen to your body and adjust if experiencing pain; consistency is more important than intensity.

## Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/weight-management-arthritis-evidence
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Weight Management and Arthritis: The Evidence
A: Weight management is an effective strategy for managing arthritis symptoms. A 5% reduction in body weight can significantly reduce knee osteoarthritis symptoms. A 10% reduction in weight can even produce benefits comparable to some medications. This is achieved through consistent, small changes, tracking outcomes like pain on waking, longest pain-free intervals, and functional improvements.

## What Sustained Remission Means in RA
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/what-sustained-remission-means-in-ra
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: What Sustained Remission Means in RA
A: Sustained remission in rheumatoid arthritis means stable minimal or no disease activity, not a cure. The article says it is a key treatment goal, often maintained through ongoing medication, monitoring, gentle regular movement and lifestyle support. It advises personalised clinician guidance, symptom tracking, pacing activity, and prompt review for swelling, fever, rapid function loss or medication side effects.

## Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/why-exercise-makes-your-arthritis-medication-work-better
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Why Exercise Makes Your Arthritis Medication Work Better
A: Regular physical activity, including strength training, can make arthritis medication more effective by reducing pain, improving physical function, and enhancing quality of life. This integrated approach, which combines medication with movement, is recommended in clinical guidelines. Exercise is thought to lower widespread inflammation, maintain healthy weight, strengthen muscles, and improve mood, all of which support treatment response.

## Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/your-workplace-rights-with-arthritis-the-equality-act-2010
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Your Workplace Rights With Arthritis: The Equality Act 2010
A: Arthritis can impact work performance due to its effects on physical tasks, concentration, and energy levels. Many individuals with arthritis work successfully, often with workplace adjustments. Reasonable adjustments, which are a legal entitlement, include flexible hours, ergonomic equipment, and adjusted duties. You do not have to disclose your arthritis to your employer unless it poses a health and safety risk.

## Juvenile Arthritis UK: A Parent's Guide to Childhood Joint C
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/juvenile-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Juvenile Arthritis UK: A Parent's Guide to Childhood Joint C
A: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA) is a group of autoimmune conditions causing joint inflammation in children under 16, affecting approximately 15,000 children and young people in the UK. Parents might notice limping, morning stiffness, swollen joints, or unusual irritability. Diagnosis involves clinical assessment by a paediatric rheumatologist. Treatment aims for remission, using medicines like NSAIDs, methotrexate, and biologics, alongside physiotherapy to maintain joint function and strength.

## Foot and Ankle Arthritis UK: Symptoms, Exercises and Footwea
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/foot-and-ankle-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Foot and Ankle Arthritis UK: Symptoms, Exercises and Footwea
A: Foot and ankle arthritis symptoms vary by type but commonly include pain, stiffness, and swelling. For big toe arthritis, you might notice difficulty walking and a bony bump. Ankle arthritis often causes deep pain, stiffness in the morning, and swelling. Rheumatoid arthritis in the feet can lead to pain under the ball of the foot and toe deformities, affecting up to 90% of those with RA.

A: Many gadgets and daily living aids can help people with arthritis manage tasks and reduce joint strain. Examples include ergonomic jar openers, specially designed cutlery, and kettle tippers for the kitchen. Personal care aids like button hooks and long-handled shoe horns assist with dressing. Technology such as ergonomic keyboards, voice assistants, and styluses can also make daily life easier.

## Assistive Devices for Arthritis – UK Buyer's Guide
URL: https://livingwitharthritis.org.uk/blog/assistive-devices-arthritis-uk
Last updated: 2026-06-08
Q: Assistive Devices for Arthritis – UK Buyer's Guide
A: Assistive devices can help manage arthritis by making daily tasks easier and reducing joint strain. Examples include kitchen aids like electric tin openers, kettle tippers, and ergonomic utensils. For the bathroom, grab rails, shower seats, and raised toilet seats are available. Dressing aids such as long-handled shoe horns and sock aids can assist, while mobility aids like walking sticks and wheelchairs can improve movement.
